MONK (Jacques Cartier) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 49) respecting water-powers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Explain.

The object of this Bill, Mr. Speaker, is to conserve as far as possible for our country, the great wealth of waterpower which we find that we possess. Since the creation of the commission on conservation a very active investigation has taken place by the commission in order to ascertain the extent of our forest, mineral, and water-power wealth. There have been different committees of that commission and the one concerning water-powers, with which I have the honour to be connected, during the first year of the existence of the commission, ascertained to a very considerable extent the amount of our water-power wealth throughout the country. The result of that investigation has been surprising and the stage that we have arrived at now is this: What can we do in order to preserve that immense source of wealth and industrial development for the country? In view of that, the present Bill has been prepared as an attempt at legislation in that direction. We have no legislation upon the alienation of this great source of wealth that I am aware of, and this Bill endeavours to surround that alienation with precautions that will ensure the maintenance of that wealth and its utilization, not for a select few, but for the public in general.
It provides, amongst other things, that when alienation has been decided upon,
either upon the petition of an individual or upon the action of the government, the question is submitted to the Conservation Commission in order that it shall furnish suggestions to the government as to the value of the water-power and the conditions most satisfactory for the country and for the public under which the alienation should take place. No alienation can be made otherwise than by lease which, in its duration, cannot exceed fifty years. There is no final alienation. When the Conservation Commission has made its report upon the different points of interest mentioned in the Bill, the government advertises the water-power for sale by auction under the conditions prescribed. Five years before the lease expires the government intimates to the lessee what it considers to be a reasonable condition for the renewal of the lease and within a certain space of time the lessee must state whether he accepts the condition or not. Otherwise, the waterpower site is sold at auction again under leasehold tenure and the former lessee is indemnified for his improvements or expenses. The government has power to pass rules and regulations regulating the administration of the law, and the Commission on Conservation itself has power to pass rules and regulations binding upon the departments and binding upon the lessee, obligating him to conform to certain conditions and all these, when approved of by the Governor in Council and published in the ' Canada Gazette,' become law. These are the principal dispositions of this new Bill.
There is a final section which says that all alienations hitherto made by the government of water-powers where the lessee or the grantee, under whatever title, has not conformed to the conditions of the alienation, either by failure to pay rent or to develop, or to conform in other respects to the conditions of the instrument of alienation, will, after the coming into force of this Act, become void absolutely, and the government can take possession once more of the powers and deal with them under the disposition of the new law. The Conservation Commission meets at the beginning of the month of January and this Bill cannot come up for the second reading until after that meeting and until after the government has had time to consider it. It seems to me that it is absolutely necessary for us, in face of the inventory we have made showing the extent of our wealth in that respect to make some provision to prevent any wasteful alienation of this source of wealth.

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) is somewhat in error in stating that there is no legislation on this subject. If my hon. friend will refer to the Dominion Lands Act, 1908, he will find legislative provisions there for dealing

with water-powers under the jurisdiction of the Dominion government, and based upon that legislative authority, granted by parliament in 1908, regulations have been provided for dealing with water-powers under the control of the Dominion which have been availed of to a very considerable extent, and which, I think, on careful examination will be found to have served the public interest to the fullest possible extent that my hon. friend can suggest in his Bill.

I have not recently seen the account referred to by my hon. friend, but this much I know, that it is very incomplete indeed, and that the regulations that have been founded upon that Act are felt by those who have had any experience of water-powers to be absolutely impracticable. At any rate, the object of this Act is to bring into close contact the government and the Conservation Commission, which it has created, and to make that Commission of some use in carrying out the design of the government in creating it. The Act to which my hon. friend refers, will be found to be quite incomplete.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I wish to correct my hon. friend when he says that the regulations existing at present are incomplete or impracticable. As a matter of fact, an expenditure of millions of dollars is now under way under authority of these regulations and in accordance with their provisions.

of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) to a report given out to the press very recently to the effect that the government had decided to refuse the claim of the old settlers in the northwest, who came there between the 1st January, 1836, and the 15th July, 1870, and I would like to ask either of these hon. gentlemen whether or not it be correct that the government has finally refused to entertain their claim.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The subject to which my hon. friend refers has been brought to the attention of the government on several occasions, and quite recently it was brought to our attention by a deputation which was in Ottawa yesterday. The request is that the white settlers who came into the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta between 1836 and 1870, that is, between 1836 and the transfer of that territory to Canada, should be granted scrip just as scrip was granted to those white settlers who came in between 1813 and 1836. We have given the matter much consideration, and the decision arrived at is that as the question was settled by the parliament of Canada when it fixed the dates within which white settlers would be entitled to s.crip, which dates were from 1813 to 1836, we did not think it wise, at this distance of time, to review that decision. Another side of the question is, as it was stated the other day by my hon. colleague the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden), that the policy of this government in dealing with our public lands is that these lands shall pass into the hands of private owners only on conditions of settlement and cultivation. In other words, that such past action as might be considered the policy of the government with regard to the issue of land scrip for the settlement of claims has ceased.
I beg to give notice that I shall bring the matter before the attention of the House at the earliest convenient opportunity on going into supply.

Before the orders of the day are called, I wish to ask the attention of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and the hon. the Minister
House in committee on Bill (No. 6) to amend the Interest Act.-Mr. Miller.

When we were discussing this measure in committee the other day, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) said that in his province the term ' extension agreement ' was not commonly used. Since then I wrote to the firm of Newsome 'and' Gilbert, law publishers, of Toronto, and asked them to send me a sample copy of the extension agreement they usually sell. They sent me a copy and said that they sell these agreements in all the provinces of Canada, but more in Ontario than in the others. The agreement is called [DOT] an agreement for extension of time undar

mortgage,' and is usually shortly referred to as an extension agreement. The hon. the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) thought that the first part of subsection 1 was not clearly worded. I am not at all wedded to the wording, although I have submitted it to two or three eminent lawyers, who agree that it is quite sufficient, and if my hon. friends think that they can improve the wording I shall. be happy to accept their improvement. I would suggest, in order to meet their objection, that the following amendment should be made:-
Strike out the words in section 10a in lines 7, 8, and 9 so that the section shall read: Whenever any principal money, interest or other money secured by mortgage, made after the passing of this Act, or by mortgage renewed by renewal or extension agreement after the passing of this Act
Did the hon. gentleman submit that to the Minister of Justice?
I did not think that was necessary. If the leader of the opposition would prefer this wording I have no objection to accept it.

The hon. gentleman slightly misapprehended the point of my objection. The point was that the term ' extension agreement ' is not ordinarily used in statutes or legal documents in Nova Scotia. Notwithstanding the authority of these law stationers, I am still constrained to adhere to that opinion after an experience of some years practising my profession in my province. The hon. gentleman's proposed amendment I shall be glad to consider. In the meantime I have had representations from Nova Scotia asking that copies of this Bill be sent to persons interested in it in that province. I have sent a number of copies and would be glad if the hon. gentleman would let his Bill stand until we can hear from these persons. I do not think that the passage of the measure will be delayed in any way thereby.

I had not the slightest intention of speaking slightingly of the hon. gentleman's knowledge of the law or practice in Nova Scotia when I made the reference to the extension agreement. As to that term, I do not know that it matters much by what name the agreement is called so long as the practice is a common one of using agreements by which the time for the payment of mortgages is extended. Let them call it by what name they will, I think the term ' extension agreement ' will clearly define what we mean. As to the request to allow this matter to stand over for a reasonable time I have not the slightest objection. I move that the committee Mr. MILLER.

Mr. SHARPE (Ontario) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 7) to amend the Companies' Act. He said: The object of this Bill is to provide for full publicity by companies as to their affairs. We are living in a commercial age, and a characteristic of that age is the rapid growth and development of corporations and companies. I admit that it is necessary to the carrying on of large enterprises to have large aggregations of capital, and, to that end, to form companies and corporations. But different people have different objects in forming companies. As the members_of a company avoid personal responsibility, it is natural that people who regard the avoidance of personal responsibility in these affairs as important should turn their business into companies. Quite frequently one main object of a person in forming a company is to avoid publicity as to his interest in the enterprise. When the public, by Letters Patent, or by private Act, creates a corporation, full publicity in connection with that company should be provided for. And this is the object of the Bill. It is the law in every province, as I understand it, that companies incorporated under the provincial authority shall make annual returns to the government as to capitalization, number of shareholders and the financial position of the concern. The Bill now before the House is taken practically verbatim- with necessary changes to suit the Dominion Companies' Act-from the Ontario Companies' Act. This Bill consists of two sections. The first provides that an annual statement shall be prepared and placed in the hands of the shareholders five days before the annual meeting. Under the Dominion Act as it now stands, companies are required to prepare an annual statement and place it in the hands of the shareholders at the annual meeting for the election of officers. I submit that that does not allow those interested sufficient time to familiarize themselves with the statement so as to be in a position to ask questions or criticise the financial statement. The clause in this Bill provides that, at least five days before the election of officers, the company shall distribute a full statement of its affairs. The next section of the Bill deals with the annual statement and summary. I confess that this may not be drafted in the best possible form; it may be within the range of possibility-even of probability-that many amendments will be suggested with a view to perfecting this measure. I would suggest, however, that the principle of the Bill should be adopted by the House, and, if necessary, the measure should be sent to

a special committee, or, possibly, to one of the regular committees, for full discussion.

Hon. members are aware that there is at present before the Supreme Court a reference to determine the question of jurisdiction in regard to company incorporation as'between the Dominion and the provinces. Now, until a decision on that question is secured from the court of last resort, it is not desirable that there should be any amendments to any essential features of the Companies' Act.
Why?

There have been a great many requests for amendments to the Companies' Act, and I believe it has been the experience of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax), as I am sure it has been the experience of many other hon. gentlemen, that legislation for special purposes very frequently leads to trouble. If the requests received from time to time for amendments of the Companies' Act were acceded to, we might find, after a decision is obtained on the question of jurisdiction, that amendments had been made in regard to matters outside the jurisdiction of this parliament. That is the chief reason. However, I was proceeding to say that the amendment embodied in the Bill of my hon. friend (Mr. Sharpe, Ontario), does not extend to the question of jurisdiction. As that hon. gentleman has explained, this proposed amendment has been taken entirely from the Ontario Companies' Act. He has indicated, and correctly indicated, that, in some respects, the amendment does not apply to the Dominion Companies' Act and would require to be materially altered. However, that is a matter of detail. I may just add that, in some respects, the amendment, in my opinion, does not go far enough. It does not provide for all the particulars which my hon. friend says should be in the hands of shareholders at an annual meeting, such as particulars obtained by an audit and verified by an auditor or other person appointed for the purpose. Nor does it provide for enforcing a penalty for failure to comply with such provisions. In other respects, it goes too far,-for instance, in not ^discriminating between a company of a private character and a company of ia public character. As mv hon. friend is aware, there are many companies which, for the purposes of their undertakings, allow their employees, under special conditions, to hold stock in the company. In the ordinary course of commercial business, it is found not to be desirable that the private affairs of these companies should be generally disclosed. That is another detail which can be threshed out in committee. I am disposed to act on the suggestion contained in the remarks of my
hon. friend from South Ontario (Mr. Sharpe), and ask that the Bill be referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce, so that the necessary changes, can be made and the amendment made applicable to the Companies' Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time and referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce.

Mr. SHARPE (Ontario) moved second reading of Bill (No. 8) to amend the Railway Act. He said: My amendment to the Railway Act is designed and calculated to amend the section in regard to express companies. Express companies have been peculiarly favoured by legislation, and the object of this amendment is to require that full publicity shall be given to any unclaimed balances or any sums that are unclaimed in their hands. I understand that there are thousands and thousands of dollars in the hands of express companies in the nature of express orders that have been purchased and never been cashed, foreign bank exchanges and foreign drafts. This amendment requires express companies, at the expiration of each year, to send in a full statement to the government of those unclaimed sums remaining in their hands.
The second amendment has to do with the custody of those unclaimed balances after the expiration of one year, requiring that, instead of those moneys remaining in the hands of the company, they shall be transferred to the government as trustees thereof until the person having a legal right thereto establishes his claim and collects them from the government. As I said, express companies have peculiar privileges under our Act, and there is no reason why these unclaimed balances and these large sums that remain in the hands should become part of their assets. The term of one year has been applied to express companies, meaning that they should not retain those moneys longer than one year. My amendment to the Bank Act provides that unclaimed balances shall remain in their hands no longer than six years. The idea of fixing one year for express companies is on account of the nature of the business they are transacting. Banking, of course, is banking business. A man deposits money in the savings bank with a view of safe-keeping and receiving interest thereon. But with regard to an express company the transaction is an entirely different one. When a man buys an express order from an express company he does not deposit his money with' the idea of safe-keeping and receiving 'any'

interest return; he buys the express order with the object of utilizing it. Consequently if he loses that order, or dies, or it is mislaid, and is never cashed in, the company gets the benefit of it. Consequently the term in this amendment is fixed only at one year, so that if these moneys remain in the hands of the express company for upwards of one year they shall then make a return to the government and the moneys shall be transferred to the government as the proper custodian thereof.
There are some features about this Bill which I think must commend it to members on both sides of the House. The principle of publicity, at any rate, even if members do not go the full extent of the Bill, should commend itself to the judgment of both parties. There is no reason why, if there is an unclaimed balance in the hands of the express company, it should not be put upon the same basis as an unclaimed balance in the bank, and the express company should report it annually to the government the same as the banks do at the present time. Whether the House will go with me so far as to say that these moneys should be transferred to the government as the custodian thereof, is another question. That might be considered by a special committee. Let the Bill receive its second reading, and then be passed on to the Railway Committee, or some special (committee, which may fully discuss the principle of the Bill.
I would like to ask my hon. friend if it provides some form of procedure by which the claimant may establish his claim?
No, that would be a matter of departmental regulation. I think details of that kind could not ba profitably set out in the Bill.

There are probably some merits in this Bill, although I admit I do not thoroughly understand it as well as I would like to. The returns my hon. friend requires to be made by the express companies seem to me to be along the line of the returns made by banks. There is a difference in the interval allowed for accounting. The banks carry their balances over five years, under the Bank Act, if I am not mistaken.
They make a return every year.

But the amount of the balances is accounted for every five years. I will not enter into a discussion of the Bill now. The suggestion of my hon. friend seems quite reasonable, and we might refer it to the Railway Committee.
The Banking and Commerce Committee?

Possibly. It must be remembered that this is a Railway Bill, it is to amend the Railway Act, because the express companies have been brought under the Railway Act in order to make them amenable to the Board of Railway Commissioners. It might be well to send the Bill to the Railway Committee and from there to a sub-committee, most of whom would be members of the Banking and Commerce Committee.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

Mr. CARVELL moved the second reading of Bill (No. 9) to amend the Inspection and Sale Act. He said: The object of this Bill was set out to some extent at its first reading. It is simply to provide that when potatoes are offered for sale by the barrel, the barrel should contain 160 pounds. We have no standard under our Inspection and Sales Act for the sale of potatoes by the barrel. We have a standard of 60 pounds to the bushel, and there is also a provision that in the province of Quebec when potatoes are offered for sale by the bag, the bag shall contain at least 90 pounds. That went on for some time, and no hardship resulted. About five or six years ago the people of New Brunswick commenced to send potatoes in large quantities to the markets of Quebec and Ontario, and there, by custom, they are sold entirely 'by the bag, a bag containing by custom, not by law, 90 pounds. The result was that the merchants put two bags together and called them a barrel, and by custom potatoes, in the province of New Brunswick, and I think also in portions of Nova Scotia, are bought entirely by the barrel. As long as those potatoes were sold in Quebec and Ontario by the pound it didn't make much difference, because if a merchant bought 180 pounds and sold two bags for a barrel, that made 180 pounds and no hardship was suffered. But during the last two years especially a very large business has been worked up in Cuba. I may say that from my own constituency last year there were at least 200,000 barrels shipped to Cuba, and from the whole province of New Brunswick quite 300,000. This year there is a large quantity being sold also, and some are going not only to Quebec and Ontario, but as far west as Calgary. It works out in this way : When a farmer sells potatoes by the barrel to a merchant it must contain 180 pounds. The merchant sends a barrel of those potatoes to Quebec and Ontario, in which he gives 180 pounds to the barrel.

He sends another barrel of those potatoes to Cuba. At the present time the United States market will not admit Canadian potatoes. When he sends potatoes to Cuba he gives 160 pounds to the barrel. The result is that the merchant is saving 20 pounds on every barrel of potatoes he buys, which he sells to Cuba. I think the law of the United States is 160 pounds to the barrel. In some portions of Nova Scotia, I understand, potatoes are bought and sold by the bushel, but even there, when sold to the Cuban market, they are handled to a great extent by the barrel. Therefore this has become a burning question at least in New Brunswick, and I think it would be a benefit even to Nova Scotia, and no hardship anywhere else, that when by custom potatoes are bought and sold by the barrel, there should be a standard barrel, and every person then will know what he is doing. I realize that the merchant who buys by the barrel of 160 pounds does not, of course, sell again by the barrel if the goods are going to Quebec or Ontario. He sells by the bag, but if he sells the goods to go to the United States he sells by the barrel. He makes no profit out of the farmer to which he is not entitled and he is under no disability when selling to the other markets.

In many places in New Brunswick, and especially in Victoria and Madawaska purchasers, going around buying potatoes, say: We will pay so much for a barrel of potatoes and a barrel contains three bushels. A flour barrel contains less than three bushels, or about two and a half bushels. I want to establish the point that the purchasers of potatoes really pay for two and a half bushels and get three. I think that if there were a standard measure established all through Canada those who are interested in the shipping of potatoes would be benefited by it and I therefore support the Bill of my hon. friend.

Motion agreed to. Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
What minister is this under?

I do not know anything about the local conditions in the various provinces, and I offer no opinion as to this measure, but, I think the minister in charge of the department which administers this Act ought to give us some information on the subject, or else the Bill should stand over.

Just before the minister replies, I may state that last year I gave notice of a motion, but at the request of the Department of Trade and Commerce
I withdrew it, and this very section was incorporated in an amendment brought down to this House by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) acting for the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright). On account of the press of business during the latter part of the session that government Bill was withdrawn, I had not sufficient time in which to bring the matter up and the result was that it went over. I went to the Minister of Agriculture before the session opened and he told me that he was very much in favour of the principle and advised me to introduce this Bill myself as a public Bill. I have done so, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that both the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce are fully acquainted with the provision of the Bill and, in so far as I know, are entirely in accord with it. If you look at the records of the last session of the House you will find a Bill introduced by the Minister of Agriculture containing this exact provision.
The minister or some one ought to say so.

Mr. MONK moved the second reading of Bill (No. 11) respecting Co-operative Credit Societies.
There are some things in this Bill to which I am opposed.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
Mr. MONK moved that the House go into committee on the Bill. He said: Perhaps my hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) would like to look over the Bill before it takes the committee stage. The Bill was thoroughly examined by the Banking and Commerce Committee, and reported favourably. I do not see my hon. friend here now. It is in charge of the Secretary of State, and he may perhaps wish to look it over, although it has been carefully examined by Mr. Mulvey.
My hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) informs me that he is quite agreeable to have the Bill go through the committee to-day.

Motion agreed to, and House went into committee.
On section 5,
Under this Act, societies may be incorporated having for their object or purpose the receiving of moneys on deposit from members and the making of loans to members with or
without security, defined by the petition signed on application for incorporation.

This section gives unlimited power of receiving deposits, which I do not think is contained in any other Act. There is no restriction on the amount _ at all. Further on it is provided that this company may be incorporated by seven persons with one paid up, one dollar, share, apiece. Then they can lend money to themselves with or without security and the amount of money they may take on deposit is absolutely unlimited.

My hon. friend is mistaken in regard to that. There is this limitation, that the only depositors in the funds of the society are the members themselves. That is the rule that obtains in co-operative societies all over the world. The Bankers' Association declared, when this proviso was inserted in the Bill, that they had no objection whatever, to the incorporation, if the taking of deposits and the making of loans were restricted to the members themselves. There was inserted last year by the Banking Committee, a special clause, saying that the minister administering the Bill, that is the Secretary of State, may limit the number and amount of deposits even by shareholders, so that the point of my hon. friend is absolutely badly taken.
No, it is true that the money can be received on deposit from a member only, and loaned only to a member, but all that is required of any one in order to become a member is to pay one dollar.
Where do you find that?
The shares may be $1 apiece.
There is no such provision in the Act, by paying a dollar.
The shares may be $1 and seven may be the incorporators.
In all the big banks too, they do very strange things sometimes.

They do. If I wanted to borrow a large sum of money from this company, the company having been incorporated and in existence and receiving deposits of money, I could not borrow that money unless I was a shareholder; but I could become a shareholder, with the consent of the directors, by paying one dollar or taking one $1 share. I say that is no protection at all. This legislation is quite right, if it is carried out in the spirit and the meaning of this Act, but I say that this Act gives an opening for the worst kind of wild cat companies that it is possible to conceive. I understand from the promoter of the Bill that it is intended for the establishment of banks in certain Mr. KING
localities in the province of Quebec, and that it will be a most useful Bill in the districts where it is desired; what I object to, is the possibility of applying this Bill to Ontario and to mining companies and to promoters who would take advantage of such an Act. I say it opens the door to the wildest kind of companies, something which should be most carefully guarded against.
If I remember rightly, the Finance Minister last year was very much exercised about that power, and thought it might be got over by strictly limiting the capitalization in each case, to whatever might be the requirements of the locality, and then from time to time the capital might be increased with the consent of the Minister of Finance, if it was shown that it was going to meet the requirements of the localities where the organizations were brought into effect and required; but without some such restriction as that, this Bill gives the wild-catt promoters and the man who wants to swindle the public, the opportunity of doing it, as no other Bill on the statute-book of Canada does. It would enable any seven people in any locality in Ontario to devise a scheme for the defrauding of the public and to carry it out successfully.

I do not see why my hon. friend insists in maintaining that by paying a dollar a man can glide into these societies and organize frauds that have never been practised anywhere and which he fears can only be practised in the province of Ontario. This is a form of law which has obtained in every country which has adopted co-operation. They have it in England, in France, in every country, and it is not right to say that by paying in one dollar you can get into such a society. You must become a shareholder. Under what conditions can you become a shareholder? Not by paying a dollar, but by applying for admission into the society and fulfilling whatever conditions may be prescribed for entrance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the amount of the share?
The shares are fixed by the statute of incorporation, but they may be $5, $10 or $100.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Or they might be $1.
They might be $1.
It is provided that the share shall not be less than $1, so it may be $1.

It is not conceivable that one could attach such a small criterion as $1. The objection of my hon. friend was submitted to the Banking Committee last

year, gone into fully and overruled, because it was not thought right to refuse in this country the privilege of co-operation because frauds might be committed. Every precaution has been taken, the law has been extended so as to cover every possible attempt at fraud. The minister has continuous control over all the operations of the society. He has a right to inform himself of what the society is doing and to control its operation, but it is no more possible to exercise fraud and crime with a society organized in this way than it is in the large banks, where fraud has been committed every day by wealthy people. The public is robbed in spite of whatever may be in the law. Because it might be possible, because it is conceivable that some gigantic fraud might be made under this system of law, are we going to refuse" the public of Canada the advantages of cooperation? If my hon. friend supposes that a society composed of seven men, who would have each put in $1, might be able to obtain deposits all over the country and perpetrate the most gigantic frauds on a capital of $7, I do not anticipate that the people in our province of Quebec or in any other province of the Dominion would be liable to be led astray by such capitalization as that.

The question of capitalization does not count for very much nowadays. You see every day trust companies holding out their prospectuses and receiving deposits and issuing debentures with no capital stated and no directors named, incorporated by Act of parliament. The object of this Bill, as I understand, is to enable the organization of comparatively small co-operative concerns, absolutely proper and good, and of a nature that should be established. On the other hand, this Bill does not limit it to working in that way. This Bill says that:-
A society may create a capital divided into shares, and the amount thereof, the number of shares and the calls or other payments thereon, shall he determined by its rules, but the amount of each share shall not be less than one dollar. I
I am not assuming for a moment that the object of the promoter of this Bill is to permit the organization of companies that would allow fraud to be perpetrated or outside shareholders to come in promiscuously; but it is provided that no member shall have more than one vote, so that a man with one share would have the same voting power as a man with 10,000 shares. I am not assuming that there will be mismanagement in the honest intention of the men who organize societies under this Bill; but it happens continually that men come
into such societies deliberately to perpetrate a fraud. Under the Bill seven men can become incorporated and open an office, and they can say that they are incorporated under an Act passed by the Dominion parliament. They are not obliged to say what their capital is. They may borrow all the money that people may be willing to deposit with them; they mav borrow without limitation as to amount, and without limitation of interest. We have had cases in Canada of ordinary companies sending men out all over the country from Halifax to Vancouver to canvass for deposits, and these men have been getting a commission of 20 per cent on all the money they got, to the extent of millions of dollars. One of these companies at Toronto had respectable men connected with it; I think it had 10,000 and 15,000 shareholders in Canada. That company has for several years been in process of being wound up by the National Trust Company; and its manager was tried and sentenced to penitentiary. It is much more difficult for such a company to obtain money at present than it would be for a company incorporated under this Act. We have a very strong speculative element in Canada, and a great many unscrupulous men are exploiting that element. Under this Act seven men may form themselves into a company without capital, get a license and open offices. Then they can advertise that they are entitled to take deposits under a special Act of the Dominion parliament; and they are entitled to lend the money so deposited on any security, personal or real estate, or without any security. All that is necessary is to make the borrower a shareholder in the company; and, as the shares are only one dollar, the borrower, by paying one dollar, may take all the funds of the society without any restrictions whatever. That may occur after hundreds of thousands of dollars have been obtained from the public, and before the year is up when the statement required by the Act has to be sent to the government, the fraud may be committed, and the unfortunate depositors may be left with nothing. I would like to see this Bill meet the requirements which I know its promoter has in view; but I am perfectly certain that the Minister of Finance was exceedingly anxious about it, and was giving serious consideration to the question how he could approve the Bill and at the same time have some check over its operation. The check suggested was that the license should limit the capital of a company to whatever might be the requirements of the locality. From time to time that capital could be increased by order in council, if necessary. But if this Bill is passed as it is now, you will simply be placing a premium upon fraud, from one end of the country to the other, where-

ever a combination of seven men choose to form one of these societies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There seems to be force in the objection of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier). There may be an answer to his objection, but I do not think the answer has been given in anything that has been said by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier. My hon. friend observed that there might be fraud on the part of any corporation, however big it might be. We know that there have been frauds and losses in connection with banks with large capital. But the answer of the hon. member for West Toronto is that the difference between one of these companies and a bank is that the bank has a large capital stock in its treasury, which is a guarantee to the depositors. The hon. member for West Toronto points out, to put an extreme case, that we provide here for the organization of a company which may have nothing but merely nominal capital. Seven members can organize a company, and as the shares may be one dollar each, all the capital stock of the company may be but seven dollars; and upon that the company is allowed to borrow hundreds or thousands of dollars, and all that the depositors have to depend upon is the capital of seven dollars. To that objection there may be a good answer, but the only answer I have heard from my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier is that the experience of Europe, where such laws are in vogue, has not shown that there is ground for any such fear. Even if that be so, it does not destroy the strength of the objection made by the hon. member for West Toronto; and I know, as he has said, that the Minister of Finance has the matter in mind, and, if I recollect well, he was not altogether satisfied that there was not some danger. I suggest that my hon. friend had better let that clause stand so that the department might, be consulted in the matter.

I have no objection, if it be the desire of the right hon. gentleman, to let this clause stand, but I desire to say a few words with reference to the measure itself. I did suppose that, after having been presented to the House five or six times in five or six years and after it had been shorn last year of every possible objection, after its operations had been limited to credits among the members of the society itself, we would meet with no more objections. The main opposition we have had has come from the retail dealers, a very powerful organization. Every year when we ask for this legislation at the request of the labour and agricultural societies throughout the country we are met by the retail dealers association and our attempts are defeated. Last year we restricted the Mr. OSLER.
measure to co-operative credit societies. It, went before the Banking and Commerce Committee. The Minister of Finance was present at the meetings, ne watched the progress of the Bill, and he did not dissent from the final decision of the committee to approve it, after the assistant Secretary of State had carefully gone over its provisions from a legal standpoint and put it into shape to avoid any objections. It is therefore rather disheartening to find this year the hon. member for Toronto West, (Mr. Osier) objecting again to that clause after he had objected unsuccessfully to it last year before the committee. My hon. friend supposes an extreme case and he might just as well suppose a similarly extreme case under our Banking Act. But he does not speak of the possibility under our Banking Act of banks perpetrating huge frauds throughout the country. We know however, that some of them have done so, and we shall have to alter that Banking Act if we want to avoid such frauds. There is no such danger under the legislation I am proposing. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister spoke of the possibility of a company with $7- capital obtaining deposits throughout the country and making large loans. But how could that be possible under this Bill? A credit and loan company is organized for a particular locality. Its locality is strictly circumscribed, it is limited to a certain village or town which is defined by the Secretary of State at the time of incorporation, and outsjde that locality it cannot carry on its operations. It is also obliged to render an account whenever the Finance Minister requires one. It is obliged every year to send in a statement of its deposits and loans, at any time the minister may insist on its giving a special return, and at any moment he can cancel the society or suspend its operation, so that it is continually under his immediate control. These societies have been organized in other countries and have been eminently successful and do a great deal of good among the poor people. They are to be found in the United States, England, Germany, Denmark-in fact in all the civilized countries of the world. Why then cannot we have them in Canada? Is there greater risk in Canada in allowing our people to continue and form credit and loan societies than there is to other countries? We are told by one hon. gentleman that if we grant incorporation similar to that given in other countries, we will see this country sink under an ocean of fraud. But what evidence is there of that? My hon. friend (Mr. Osier) has referred to a loan society in Ontario, organized under the Ontario law, which had power to do business and did business everywhere, which did obtain loans in every city and defrauded the people. But what analogy is

there between a company of that kind, and the kind contemplated by this Bill? Cooperation is something due to the poor; it is something which our labouring classes have been demanding during ten years. Any number of resolutions have been sent the government asking for this legislation, and it is legislation calculated to do an immense amount of good. I do not think that we should object and prevent its passage particularly at its present stage simply because an hon. gentleman, who is interested in another form of banking totally different and who has very little experience of this particular kind of banking, stands up and declares it is dangerous.

As far as this Bill is concerned, I think it will be most dangerous. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) says that it is supposing an extreme case when we suppose that seven men, contributing each $1 to the stock, may be incorporated into a loan and credit company. But suppose 7,000 men become incorporated, each contributing $1, you will then have a capital of $7,000, and might obtain deposits amounting to $2,000,000 or $3,000,000. Whether your capital be $7 or $7,000, which in such case would make practically no difference. My hon. friend points out that the Secretary of State has authority to have the books and business inspected at any time. Well, that might be a further aid to the company in defrauding the public. They might put that into their circulars and other advertisements so as to convince the public that, as this society is under government inspection and the minister may inspect it at any time, it is a very safe place in which to deposit money. That provision would therefore increase rather than diminish the danger. My hon. friend says that, under the Banking Act, banks sometimes defraud the people, but that only goes to show that, take what precautions we may, people will be sometimes defrauded, and it only is a lesson for us to be all the more caTeful to protect people against possible fraud. The hon. gentleman further says that a great precaution is in the fact that the loans can be made only to members of the society. That, however, does not mean anything. Suppose a man applies for a loan of $100 and is told that he must be a member of the society before he can get it. He will at once pay in his dollar and become a member. We had an instance of this possibility of easily defrauding the public in the hon. gentleman's own city of Montreal, where a man named Sheldon, without the protection of any legislation, defrauded the people of many, millions of dollars. We do not want any repetition of this, and I cannot think of anything that would better aid a repetition of Sheldonizing than this proposed legislation. My hon. friend gave us to understand that the Minister of Finance
consented to this legislation before the Banking and Commerce Committee last session.
Certainly.

I cannot take that conclusion simply because he was in the habit of attending the meetings of the Banking and Commerce Committee. I am not sure whether he was present at the meeting at which this Bill finally passed or not. But I know that that particular Bill was before the committee at many sittings last session, and that it was with very great reluctance the majority consented to allow it to pass at all. And they did so, I think, more out of sympathy with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), who had, several times before, had the Bill before the committee. I believe they thought it would be well to allow the Bill to pass to be more freely discussed when it came to the House for third reading. I do not think the Minister of Finance was ever personally in favour of this legislation. True, we know that, on more than one occasion, the Committee on Banking and Commerce has gone contrary to the expressed wishes and opinions of the Minister of Finance, and has done things to which he was utterly opposed. I think he was opposed to this legislation, at any rate that he was not at all an advocate of it. I agree with the view expressed by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier). I do not think that hon. gentleman has spoken against this Bill because he was afraid that any institution that he is connected with would suffer by it, but because his great knowledge and experience of financial affairs has led him to believe, as I think any man of financial experience must see, that this is exceedingly dangerous legislation.

It is only fair for me to say that I understand this matter as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) does. I understood, last session, when this question was brought up in the Banking and Commerce Committee, that the committee was agreeable to this legislation, and the Minister of Finance was agreeable to it also, in the form in which it was finally settled. I asked the hon. member for Jacques Cartier whether the Bill, as proposed, reads verbatim the same as the one passed last session by the Banking and Commerce Committee, and he tells me that it does. I am not particularly interested in this Bill, except that I was a member of the committee, and I think it only fair that I should make a few points plain as I understood them. In the first place, this Bill was intended to allow incorporation only for one electoral district. That is to say, a society incorporated for the city of Ottawa could neither take money from nor lend money to a person who did not live in the city of Ottawa.
It is not so provided, I think.

That is the way the Bill read at first, at any rate. There was objection to that from both points of view. Some people said it might be desired to cover two electoral districts, and on the other hand it was said that an electoral district might be too large a 'territory. It was suggested to limit it by districts-giving each society -a -territory of not more than so many miles across. But it was thought that that was not practicable. _ It was agreed, and provided, under section 29, that the minister, when giving the certificate of incorporation, should limit the district within which the society might carry on its business. I think that the Bill was first made to read that the minister ' shall ' limit. All the members of the committee felt that the work of one of these societies should be strictly limited to a specified area; and, under this section, we leave it in the hands of the minister to see that that is done. Another point is covered by section 33, which provides that the society shall neither lend money to nor accept a deposit from any person who is not a shareholder. If a company were incorporated for my county, for instance, Argenteuil, it could only do business in the county, and it could neither borrow nor lend money anywhere else, nor could it go outside its own membership. The feeling of the committee, as I understood it, was that neighbours in a country district'-for this is peculiarly adapted to the country, though it could be used in the city as well-would know one another's circumstances and could safely bring in their funds to such a society knowing that the money could be loaned only to members. It would be a small society with a limited area and could not go beyond the county to do business. I certainly would oppose this in every possible way if it were permitted to these people to go all over Canada to do business- that would be an utterly impossible situation. But, take, for instance, one township in my county. I cannot see what harm would be done if, in that township, a few men went together, put in their little savings and lent them to those of their number who had use for money. If the area is not sufficiently limited under section 29, make it still stronger in this respect. The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller), who is chairman of the Committee on Banking and Commerce, said that this Bill was passed last session out of sympathy with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. That is not my recollection at all. I understood that the members and also the Minister of Finance were satisfied with the Bill in the shape in which it was passed, and the committee reported it with the hope that it would go through this House.
How would you limit this as to distance? The charter covers the entire province, as I understand it.

Section 29 of the Bill provides that the minister, by certificate of incorporation, may limit the district within which the society may carry on business. The intention was that the minister should limit it. Suppose a society were incorporated for the city of London, it would neither receive deposits nor lend money outside the limits of the city.

I do not see why Woodstock, Strathroy or any other town should not have a similar society. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk! referred to the loan societies of Ontario. I do not think that is fair. We have a large number of loan societies, but each of them has a capital of $1,000,000 or more, and these societies are limited as to deposits, according to their capital, and generally are on a very different basis from the societies as proposed here. This society has no stated capital, nor is it limited in the amount it may take on deposit. I think it is a very dangerous thing. It might work out very well in the province of Quebec, but I do not see that it could be useful in the province of Ontario. In our province, any man who has any property at all can get a loan when he requires it at very favourable rates. The effect of these institutions would be to interfere with the work of the loan societies. In the city of London we have three or four loan societies, each with *a capital of from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000. They loan money at favourable rates. I have not at hand the exact facts as to how they are limited in their deposits 'and in their borrowing powers, but these points are carefully guarded. But a society such as is proposed here could be composed of seventy men putting up $1 apiece, and they could receive any amount of money.
Only from their own members.
But anybody can become a member, and they could loan any noney of depositors practically without any security at all.

According to my memory, this Bill was the subject of a great deal of discussion in the Banking and Commerce Committee last year. I do not remember whether clause 5, as we have it before us now, is the same as it was passed last year : I take the word of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that it is. But I must say that it looks to me like a very dangerous clause, as illustrated by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), who has had a great deal of experience in this sort of

thing, and whose opinion I value in questions of finance. My memory is, answering the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Per-ley), that we did pass the Bill through committee ; and I told my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier that I agreed to its going through the committee, in order that it might be well discussed in this House, (but that so far as I was personally concerned, I would oppose it in the House. I think he remembers that. The main clause I objected to was clause 24 allowing the withdrawal of capital. I thought that was a most dangerous clause, and I distinctly remember telling my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier that I would oppose that in the House.

, When the Bill was before the Banking and Commerce Committee last year it was regarded generally as a dangerous measure. It is true that it has been somewhat improved since it was first brought before the committee, but it still seems to me a dangerous measure. I do not care to say very much against it, in view of my relation with many financial institutions, for fear that I might be accused of opposing the Bill from some sinister motive. But relieving myself of that charge, I desire to say that I think clause 29 is a very dangerous clause. It may be all right in the province of Quebec, and in some of the smaller provinces, but it would not be desirable as a Dominion law. Now clause 29 says :
The minister by the certificate of incorporation and notice thereof in the ' Canada Gazette/ may limit the district within which a society may carry on its business by means of offices or other places for carrying it on, or by means of agents, canvassers or otherwise.
Now, supposing an application came in from the city of Montreal, or the city of Toronto, or the city of Winnipeg, or the city of Vancouver, from an association of seven persons, and toy a small subscription on their part offices are opened and they begin to take deposits and advertise themselves as a loan company, with the powers of a loan company, practically with the powers of a bank. Then the clause referred to toy the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has to be taken into consideration, under which a part of the capital may be withdrawn at any time. So that a person depositing in one of these co-operative institutions, if I understand it correctly, has no means of knowing what the real capital of the company might be. I think the measure is a dangerous one. If it is to become law it should be surrounded with such conditions as would inform the public exactly what the capital really is. I only make these one or two criticisms, because I do not mean to say that 42
I am opposed to the Bill if it is surrounded with the necessary safeguards. But at present, it is open to criticism, and liable to deceive the public as to its capitalization and regular order of business.
I am willing to accept the suggestion of postponing the consideration of the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Only that clause, we can go on with the other sections.

I am afraid that the committee as constituted, has not looked over the Bill carefully. It is not a Bill to organize loan societies, it is a Bill to permit poor people to help themselves locally by co-operation. The general idea seems to be in the committee, judging from what we have heard, that this is a scheme for making money. My right hon. friend knows enough about co-operation to know that it is no such thing. It is ito permit seven or more poor men in a village, in a small parish, or in any locality, on application to the minister, to put their liittJe resources together for mutual assistance, instead of having to submit to money shavers to get the accommodation they require. If you start with the idea that it is a scheme to organize a financial company, to make loans, to obtain deposits, you depart altogether from the principle of co-operation. I would suggest that the further consideration of the Bill be postponed; because, if we go on to consider other clauses, we will always be coming back to the discussion of the principle involved, which is one of mutual help amongst poor people, not a money making scheme at all. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), submitted this Bill to the Bankers' Association, with the result that he was satisfied when it came before the Banking Committee., I do not know if the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy), was present at the last meeting. I am not aware that the Bill was passed by the committee merely for my own sake. Although I am a poor man, I am not poor enough to need the assistance of this parliament. This Bill is asked for by a large class of the population in all the provinces. It is not a Bill for the province of Quebec alone, as some hon. gentlemen seem to think, it is a Bill that has been in successful operation in England, Scotland, France, Germany, Italy, in fact in every other country except this one. It seems to be capable of working successfully everywhere, except in the province of Quebec, and probably, in the city of Toronto.

I think the hon. member for , Jacques Cartier is mistaken. Certainly for my part, I am entirely in sympathy



with the object of the Bill. I think the object of the Bill is one that ought to be provided for, either by this Bill or some other. We must consider what the effect of it might be by designing persons getting hold of the powers conferred by the Bill. In discussion before the committee the question was asked as to the probable amount of capital that would be accumulated under it, and I think the answer was that $20,000 would be a large amount, and $80,000 would be the ultimate sum that these societies have in view. I say without any hesitation, that as the Bill is drawn now, it will facilitate fraud. No doubt within three weeks after the passing of the Bill, there will be 50 societies incorporated, with officers and canvassers going round to get money.

I do not wish to discuss the merits of this Bill, but I want to utter a slight word of protest as to the method in which it has come before the House. It seems to me that the Prime Minister himself, has always taken the position that this House should accept the recommendations of the standing committees which were expressly constituted for the purpose of sifting out all the difficulties and objections, and drawbacks to the various measures that are brought before those committees, in order to facilitate the work of the House. Now the member for South Grey has laid down an entirely new doctrine, that is the reverse of flattering, either to the committee or to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. He has stated that this Bill, after an elaborate discussion before the committee, after close scrutiny, was reported to the House out of sympathy for the member for Jacques Cartier. If it was reported for that purpose, the sympathy was withdrawn after it got into the House. But the fact remains that the Bill was reported and actually receive the sympathy* and endor-sation of ministers during its discussion in committee. Yet, after passing the committee and coming to this House, hon. gentlemen, including even the member for South Grey, who was chairman of the committee, get up and discover that it is the most dangerous measure that was ever brought before the House. I do not think with all due deference, that these hon. gentlemen have done justice to the hon. member who has introduced the Bill or to the hon. members of the House, who are satisfied to take the report of the standing committee.

I did not introduce any new principle. Last session there was a certain Bill before the House that was referred to a special committee who reported almost unanimously in favour of the Bill. I remember that the right hon.

Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) voted, according to the finding of that committee, for the Bill, but that the majority of the House voted against it. I do not know whether that principle was ever introduced before or not, but certainly it was introduced and acted upon last session, so that it is not a new position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is quite evident that in this House we are all in favour of the principle of the Bill, evert the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr., Osier). But the Bill, I understand, wast considered by the Banking Committee and reported favourably last session. That ought to be sufficient-it is for me, at all events-but when a gentleman so eminent in the world of finance suggests the reconstruction of a clause which has been adopted, even by the Banking Commit-* tee, I think, in the absence of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), I owe it to the House to say that the Department of Finance should be consulted as to the effect of this clause. It may be that the Finance Minister ha^ come to the conclusion that the danger that appears upon the face of it would be eliminated from the fact that this Bill is intended to apply only in one locality1 simply amongst friends, men who know each other, and it may be that thfe Department of Finance may have come to the conclusion that the Bill should be allowed to pass. I simply suggest that) this clause should be allowed to stand so1 that I may consult the Department ofi Finance and have their view upon it. If my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) prefers that the matter shall not be proceeded with until we consult with the Department of Finance, well and good. I have suggested that Tve might go on with the other clauses, but if my hon. friend prefers that no progress be made until this point is settled, I am in his hands as far as that goes.
I am quite ready to pro-* ceed.	I

My impression in the committee last session was that a great many clauses were passed because of the opposition of a certain individual whoi seemed to turn the proceedings into a' sort of burlesque. As soon as a clause' was read he would get up and offer objections, but the clause would be carried apparently regardless of him. He was the one who appeared to be fighting the Bill and the committee did not take much stock in what he said. But the impression left on my mind was this: Whereas the Bill is intended for a good purpose, and probably, if honestly worked

out by honest people, would effect a good purpose, dishonest people might make use of it for a very bad purpose and get capital out of people. Designing people could go to others and influence them to join a_society, pay in $1 or $5 each, and by promises of large interest on the money deposited in this society induce individuals to deposit a lot of money. They might deposit just as much as any designing person could get them to deposit. Supposing that half a dozen people wefle working together, that the limit of this society was the limit of the city of Toronto, that they got a thousand people in Toronto to join the society and put in $5 or $1 apiece, with perhaps a dozen people becoming members of the society and putting in $10,000 or $20,000, what is there in the Bill to prevent these individuals lending the money out between themselves and dividing it up? As far as I can see there is nothing at all. The provisions of the Bill would seem to be capable of allowing such fraudulent transactions to take place that afterwards the community would wonder that such a thing should be allowed in the country. I think that is the dangerous part of it. I have seen no clause in the Bill that would provide a sufficient safeguard against this danger.

I am not taking a different course with respect to this Bill from that which I pursued last year. I was opposed to it last year because I did not think the Bill was wanted in the province of Ontario where we have no necessity for suoh a Bill. I would like to ask on what security this money would be loaned. Suppose a gentleman comes and asks for a loan of $5,000 or $6,000, what security is he required to give?
He takes it without giving any security.
I would be very sorry to have any money of mine in a concern that would simply give a man a thousand dollars and take his note for it.
Does my hon. friend (Mr. Beattie) ask if a stranger coming to the society could get a loan?
No, but one of themselves.
A member of the society coming to the society for a loan could only get the money from his associates.
By paying $1 he becomes an associate.

Does my hon. friend say that by paying $1 he is entitled to go and get a loan of $5,000?
42i

There is nothing in the Bill about the security which he would give for the money that he would borrow, so that it is unguarded in that way. The members of the board might lend the money amongst themselves.

The remarks of my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the discussion that has taken place in the House, demonstrate, I think, the wisdom of acting on the suggestion made by the right hon. the Prime Minister of proceeding with the Bill clause by clause. The hon. member for East Grey has just said that he did not see sufficient safeguards in the Bill. The safeguards of one kind and another will become apparent to the committee as it proceeds. The hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) spoke a moment ago of how the operations of these societies are restricted, first, as to area of operations. He pointed out further wherein their operations are limited as respects the number of people who can borrow or lend in connection with each society. But there are two or three other sections of the Bill to which attention has not been drawn in the committee. Section 35 says:-
Every society shall, at its first general meeting, elect from its members a board of credit of at least three members who shall not be members of the committee or board of supervision or officers of the society, and the president of the society shall be an ex officio member of such board.
2.	The members of the board shall hold office for three years and until their successors are appointed. One-third of the members of th board, who, in the first two years and until the order of seniority begins, shall be chosen by lot, shall retire annually, but shall be eligible for re-election.
3.	No member of the board shall borrow from or be in any way liable to the society.
Then subsection 4:-
4.	It shall be the duty of the board to consider and approve of all loans and investments of funds of the society.
In other words, the only men who can borrow from the society are men who have put some of their own money into it. When a member applies to the society for a loan, the loan has to be approved of by a board chosen by all those in the first instance who put their money into me society, approved of by that supervisory board. But there is a further clause, section 36, which says that there shall also be a board of supervision, and in subsection 3 it is provided :-
The board shall, from time to time, ex amine and audit the books of the society and deposit books of the members; shall supervise the operations of the committee and board of credit; and shall check the cash investment* and securities of the society.

So that you have, first of all, the work of the society limited to men who are known to each other, who are all living in- the same locality, being able only to borrow money which they themselves put into the society, all loans supervised by a committee which they have chosen for that very purpose, and this committee in turn supervised by another committee chosen also from those members who are working altogether to watch the operations of the society. I think that as the committee proceeds with the Bill these various sections which have been inserted to meet just the situation which has been pointed out by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) will become apparent and possibly by the time we have reached the end of the Bill the members will have a very different view as to its purpose.

I had not looked at that section. But that is assuming that the incorporation under this is honest. The point that I take * is that it _ enables dishonest men to become the chief officers of the society and to check themselves. There is no check on that, whatever officers they have control the entire society, they have the appointing of the supervisors, and if they go in to deliberately defraud there is no check except,by the men whom they themselves appoint.

What provision would the hon. member (Mr. Osier) make in regard to the objection he raises? The trouble is this: The object of the society is to secure co-operative action among different parties intending to borrow money among themselves from some particular members of the community. You may make provisions such that you cannot carry on the work of the society. There must always be some risks and the question is, are the risks greater than they ought to be? If they are greater than they ought to be those who oppose the Bill should be in a position to say how they would guard against undue risk, what provisions they would make and still carry out the provisions of the Bill.
What is the primary object of the Bill? It is a co-operative society to get money cheaper for neighbours amongst themselves. You make all the provisions possible for the purpose of guarding against frauds of any kind, but you may make so many provisions that you cannot loan the money. The trouble is that you cannot make it perfect, you cannot accomplish your object without running some risks. Are the risks greater than they ought to be? If they are greater than they ought to be, some one who is objecting to the Bill ought to give a practical illustration of how he intends to guard against them.

I think the risks are infinitely greater than any benefit that could possibly accrue, assuming that all the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) says is right. I think there is only one way of checking this. It was discussed last year, and I thought the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) had agreed to it. That is to strictly limit the amount of capital. It was stated by the promoters of the Bill last year that probably in any district where they proposed to organize such a society, for a year, or, perhaps, two years, the deposits, all told, would not be more than $80,000.
I never could have made such a statement. It would take them ten years to get a capital of $4,000.

Then I am not over the mark. What I gathered last year from the promoters of the Bill was that it was intended to operate in a small way among poor people with an absolutely proper object, and that it was a very good way of promoting savings. It was suggested that the Finance Minister, or whoever issued a certificate, should in the first place make some inquiry as to the district, and that the outside capital which would be obtained by borrowing should be limited to some amount, say $20,000. I think one of the men promoting the Bill gave as an outside possibility a deposit of $80,000
That is a very large exaggeration.

If that is the case, while there is, of course, a certain risk, as in all things, you absolutely prevent that Bill being applied to other parts of the country for the purpose of fraud. As the promoter of the Bill says now, $20,000 would be an outside estimate for the first capitalization. If the operations grew from year to year, application would be made to the Finance Minister and to Council and a certificate given to increase the capital, tout if we should limit what is really in the mind of the promoters of the Bill, to say $20,000 to begin with, we would have a maximum amount of money which would absolutely prevent any temptation to people elsewhere to take advantage of the Bill. That is a simple solution and if that was accepted most of the other clauses would be quite safe, and we could thoroughly trust the people who organize and go into such a society to guard themselves.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let clause 6 stand?

I -was going to suggest that it would be an advantage if members of the committee had time to read over the Bill. The Minister of Labour is familiar with this Bill tout many of the members I of this committee have not read it and I

think time would be gained if we could postpone its consideration altogether. I am in the hands of the committee. I am not seeking this legislation for myself -but for a large class of people and I would say to my right hon. friend and to the committee that similar legislation exists in almost every country. This Act is copied practically from the English Friendly Societies Act and there is similar legislation in France, Belgium, Austria, Germany and Italy ; in fact I do not know of any country in Europe where they have not such legislation. They have it now in the United States. They are passing a Bill absolutely similar to this in Massachusetts at the present time. If I mention that it is because it seems to me that if such legislation has been found useful and necessary in other countries, we can afford to consider it here. What co-operation has done in European countries is known, I suppose, to some members of this House. It has worked miracles, it has enabled poor people to get rid of shavers and others who loan money at very high rates of interest. It has completely altered the population where it has been established and helped to build up local wealth. The trouble is when one comes to consider this legislation one is apt to think that this is a society established with a view of making money. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) speaks of a limit of deposits of $80,000 or $20,000, These societies start in a small community with a capital of $200 or $300. No one would be foolish enough to deposit a large amount with a society having a capital of $200 or $300. We started one in Levis. It is twelve or fifteen years old, and it has to-day a financial movement of about $75,000 ; but that represents fifteen years of patient work in a population that is rather well-to-do and in a society that has been encouraged. In addition to the checks mentioned by the Minister of Labour, there are the returns to the minister. This legislation has for its object to permit poor people to do what big people are doing every day-organizing banks and financial associations. It establishes a link between these institutions and poor people. If hon. members of the committee will take time to read the Bill and analyze its clauses, the discussion will be shorter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the members of the committee who have not read the Bill are waiting for an opportunity to do so, this is the time. If they do not read it now, they will not read it at all. If you proceed with the Bill clause by clause, perhaps the objections will be dispelled, when we see the precautions taken to prevent aJbuse of the legislation.
On section 20,
Every officer of a society who receives or has charge of money, shall, before taking upon himself the duties of his office, become bound, either with or without a surety, as the committee may require, in a bond according to one of the forms set forth in Schedule C to this Act, or such other form as the committee approves, or shall give the security of a guarantee society, m such sum as the committee directs, conditioned for his rendering a just and true account of all moneys
received and paid by him on ^^Lunint society, at such times as its rules appoint or as the society or the committee thereot requires him to do, and for Tie Payment bj him of all sums due from him to the society.
Take the words ' either with or without a surety as the committee may require ' does that make the requiring of sureties optional?
As I understand it, there must be a bond, but the committee may say whether that bond shall be with or without surety.
I suppose that the real object is that in a locality there might be an individual acceptable to and they might allow him to take the office without giving a surety.
But a bond is obligatory.

Yes, he gives a bond. In the beginning of the society the amount received is so small, that a surety may not be required.
On section 24,
The capital of the society may, subject to the rules, he increased by subscriptions for new shares or the admission of new members, and it may he diminished by withdrawals.
Can withdrawals be made without reference to the minister?

It is absolutely necessary to allow members to withdraw or you might as well give up the whole Bill. When a man puts in his small amount, it must be understood that he is able to withdraw it when he sees fit, otherwise it would be impossible to get these societies started. That is the experience of co-operative societies throughout the world. Why should he not withdraw the amount he has put in? When he enters he pays something as a right of entry, and an amount is retained on the profits which he loses if he withdraws. All he gets back is the amount he puts in.

That is where the trouble
arose in the committee last year. It is perfectly right to allow a member to withdraw his deposit, but absolutely unfair to allow him to withdraw his membership. All the members might withdraw, and no notice is required. The hon. gentleman will not find that in the English Act.
I assure my hon. friend there is such a provision in the English Act.
I cannot find it, and I looked for it. If a man wants to leave the society, let him sell his membership, there will be no difficulty in his doing so especially if there are any profits coming to him.
