A man joins one of these societies and takes, say, a share or two. On entering he pays a small fee, and every year there is withheld a certain amount on the profits that constitute a reserve. He does not withdraw his membership fee, but only the amount he put in.
I do not want to prevent his withdrawing his deposit, but he should not be allowed to withdraw his share or right of membership.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If one can withdraw, so could any number, and how would that affect the credit of the company?

No doubt if they all combined together to withdraw on the same day, they have the right to do it. But that has never happened. A man wants his capital back and he withdraws. If you suppose that on the same day, by common consent, they all arrange to withdraw, the society is broken up. But they are all in the same box. No one can make a deposit unless he is a member, and no one can make a loan unless he is a member, and you must trust to a certain extent to their common sense. They do not withdraw in that way in other countries, and if they should they would all suffer.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) is considering what has happened in other countries, but these societies have not been in vogue in this country.
We held a long inquiry which went into the working of these companies as they exist in other countries, let my hon. friend read that.

My -hon. friend has said that these societies will serve -a good purpose in small communities among men of small means, handling small sums of money, but there is no,thing in the Act to limit the amount of shares which any one person may hold. These small communities are the very worst possible points in which to get up a panic. Until a few years ago we had in Ontario a considerable number of private banks, many of which went into liquidation, not because they were not solvent, but because for some reason or other the people became suspicious and panic ensued. Now, in just the kind of communities that my hon. friend expects -Mr. NESBITT.
these societies to operate in, if the man in charge of the funds is seen some day driving a new carriage or doing something else that his neighbours may consider extravagant, they will very likely jump to the conclusion-some of them at least,-that this is being done with the money of the society. And thus, not through conspiracy, but through fear, they may rush to withdraw the money they have put in. A panic is sure to follow. They will not be able quickly to realize on their assets, and there will be a loss, greater or smaller, as the money in the treasury may be more or less.

We have in this discussion a most anomalous position. My hon. friend from Yale-Oaribou (Mr. Burrell), brought it out in what he said with reference to the standing committees of this House. Here is a Bill reported back by the leading standing committee of this House, and the ohairman of that committee rises and opposes the very principle of the Bill. That is a thing that never occurred in this House before. The duty of the government is clear, as laid down by my hon. friend. It is to support the report of the committee unless-a very exceptional case-some amendment has been found necessary between the report and the bringing of the matter up in the House. In such a case, they should be prepared with a statement on the subject, and should move to refer the Bill back to the committee for the purpose of amendment. But surely it is an anomalous, and, fortunately, an almost unheard-of thing, for the chairman of a committee to oppose a Bill that has been passed by that committee and sent to this House for approval.

I do not think there is any anomaly in the matter. If any one member of this House has a better right than another to object to this Bill now, it is I, and for the very reason that I am chairman of the committee. This Bill was before the 'committee last year. Being in the chair, I had not an opportunity to object to it as I have to-day. But my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), must not blame me for doing that which he, himself, has done. Last session, a Bill was referred to a special committee. That committee reported favourably, but when the matter came up, he voted against the BUI and against the report of the committee.
What analogy is there between the two cases?
The cases are parallel.
Did the chairman of the committee vote against the Bill in the House?
No.

The case cited by the hon member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has not very much force here for this Bill has not been sent to a committee this session. It was last year that the Bill was submitted to a committee and reported favourably. The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) might very properly, in the meantime, change his mind with regard to the whole Bill and oppose it this session at every stage.

This section 24 should be left over, as it is one of me greatest consequence. A society may be formed for Toronto, Winnipeg or London, and may have a capital of half a million. The shareholders put in their money, and the society receives a deposit. There is nothing to prevent any large depositor from taking out his money without notice. That, surely, is not right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as I am concerned, the argument that would induce me to vote for the clause is the statement of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that this is a copy of the existing law in England. I see great force in what is stated by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier). But my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier says that the experience in England is against it and that this is a copy of the English law.

I think I am correct as to the law in England. You cannot possibly organize a society of this kind in a poor district if a man is not sure that he is able to withdraw his money when he desirese to do so. My hon. friend from West Toronto is always imagining societies of hundreds of thousands of dollars, with great depositors suddenly withdrawing their money and so on. All this is theoretically possible, I suppose, but it is not what the Bill contemplates. I will get the English law with regard to withdrawals.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The object of this Bill, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) says, is to permit a small company to be organized in a rural district among the poorer classes of the community. That is a good object. But I see great force in the objection of the hon. member for West Toronto that there is no limitation in the Bill. There is nothing to prevent speculators organizing a society on a large scale and speculating in it. _ If there were in this Bill any provision-which I fail to see-that it is to be limited only to the class of people spoken, of by the hon. member (Mr. Monk), I could see much greater force in his case. But the Bill is so framed that the objections raised by my hon. friend from West Toronto are not met.

The check against anything occurring such as is contemplated by my
hon. friend from West Toronto is in the fact that in these societies each shareholder has only one vote and there is no voting by proxy. The result is that nobody embarks any large sum of money in them. That is. essential to a co-operation society of tJi.s kind. It stands to reason, and it has been found by experience that, with a provision of this kind, no large ^capitalist or speculator will embark in the enterprise, for they have no more voting power, man for man, than the other shareholders.

There must be some mistake on the part of my hon. friend, the member for Jacques Cartier. I have here a copy of the Industrial and Provident Societies " Act of Britain, under which all the cooperative societies of that country, I think, are incorporated. Section 19 provides:
No registered society which has any withdrawable share _ capital shall carry on the . business of hanking.
I think, under the circumstances it would be well that this clause should stand to be considered when the other clauses we have reserved are taken up later.

I have no objection to that. But what my hon. friend (Mr. King) says reminds me that there are other reasons in connection with the English Act m support of this clause which I can point out when the clause comes up again.
On section 25:	, ,
Any other corporation may, if its constating instruments permit, hold shares m a society; hut the society shall not lend any part of its funds to such other corporation until the minister has given his consent to such loan.

It means that an agricultural society, for instance, may take shares, but the co-operative society shall not loan any of its funds unless the minister gives his consent to such loan. It often happens that a small agricultural society, or local circle, may desire to take some snares in this society, and it may do so, but the society itself cannot loan any funds to such corporation unless the minister permits it.
On section 26-votes and proxies.
That also applies to a small company.

Is my hon. friend opposed to voting by proxy? Because that is at the very basis of co-operation. There must be only one vote. But you must make an exception if the society happens to hold shares in a co-operative society.

All these objections should be removed. If the company is limited to the small field that it is intended to cover, that clause might pass. But if it is to apply to large companies permitted under this Bill, I think it is entirely objectionable. If

you say that the certificate issued bv the Finance Minister limits the capital to $20,000, and if evidence shows him that the business is extending satisfactorily, they may increase the capital to $40,000 or $50,000.
That is already the Act. The minister, in authorizing the company, may fix a limit beyond which it cannot go. But if my hon. friend wishes to fix it at $20,000 I am willing.
If you do not fix a limit you allow companies to be organized in Montreal or Toronto with an unlimited capitalization.

What this clause consecrates is a principle universally admitted, that there must be one vote and no proxy. We have reserved a couple of clauses which will enable us to limit the capitalization.
ance Minister to extend the privileges of these companies?
The hon. member has been arguing all the way through that this will involve only small transactions and that no large sums wall be risked.
If my hon. friend has read anything with respect to the development of these societies in Europe he will know that there has been an accumulation of a hundred million francs in some cases.

I have read a good deal and I have listened a good deal. I have listened to the claim set forth that it will only be a business of small transactions. I have listened to the hon. gentleman himself say that in Milan and elsewhere the transactions went into millions. He cannot argue one way one time and another way another; he cannot blow hot and cold.

The objection of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is fully met by the provision which requires the minister to approve of the rules, and among the rules is one stating the maximum number of shares which shall be held by a member, the maximum amount received by a society on deposit, and the maximum amount which may be received from or loaned to a member.	[DOT]
On section 27, Register of members or shares.

What is the meaning of the words ' or agreed to be considered as paid on any such shares '?
Mr. MONK moved that the words ' or agreed to be considered as paid on any such shares ' in the seventh and eighth lines be struck out.
If the intention is to confine the work to small places, why not put in a limit of $20,000? That would prevent the organization of any larger company.
The minister can always refuse to incorporate a company and'limit the scope of its operations, the Act gives him that power.
Is it the intention of the promoter that the society shall have more than one vote?
The society has but one vote, but the society votes by proxy.
If it is accepted that the capital be limited in the first issue to $20,000, I am willing to let the clause pass.

I think it should be left to the ^ minister, as suggested under the observation of the Minister of Labour. When the Finance Minister grants existence to a society, he fixes the limit beyond which it cannot go. Why should we not leave him that discretion? Why should we say that these few poor people should be limited to $20,000, although their affairs may be prospering, and that they should not go beyond $20,000, as rich people may? Why should we not treat poor people as well as rich people? In Milan, Italy, banking societies have raised their funds to millions, by dmt of perseverance and care. Why should we not leave discretion to the Fin-
Section as amended agreed to.

May I be allowed to ask a question with respect to section 26? It has been suggested that the word ' member ' might not include an incorporated company. The intention of this was that an agricultural association would only have one vote and should be counted as a member. I thought that the clause was plain enough, but it has been suggested that it should be amended so as to make it perfectly clear that no company should have more than one vote. I think the word ' member ' should be explained.
It is not explained in the interpretation.
I looked at the interpretation clause and it is not there.
It does not leave it very clear as to whether in incorporated societies there should be a number of votes corresponding to their shares or whether an individual member shall only have one vote.

The interpretation might be amended easily enough-.
On section 28, dues of members.

With regard to section 26, I move reconsideration and I propose to put in after the word ' member1 in the first line the words ' individual or corporate/ This is a point that I think should be made very clear. This is one of the main

things in this Bill which recommended it to me that no association, no matter how many shares it might hold, would have more than one vote. This is a very essential thing with regard to the Bill.

While you are reconsidering section 26, I think it is very vaguely worded in other respects.
No member shall have more than one vote, and voting by proxy

I rise to a point of order. It seems that my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) is out of order. We have reconsidered section 26 for a particular purpose and, that purpose having been disposed of, I do not think my hon. friend is at liberty to proceed.

The motion was to reconsider section 26.
No member shall have more than one vote, and voting by proxy shall be allowed only when shares are held by an agricultural association

And so on. It seems to me that one meaning that might quite clearly be taken is that when any of the shares are held by an agricultural association, a municipal body, or a school board, every person may vote by proxy. I do not want to obstruct, but I think the meaning is not clear.
I think the section is perfectly clear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is proposed to amend the first section by adding, after the word ' member,' the words ' individual or corporate.'
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the section as amended be agreed to?

I would like to have time to prepare an amendment. I, with other members sitting around me without endeavouring to obstruct the Bill, Would like to give some meaning to it and I would ask the promoter of the Bill whether he does not think that the meaning that I have suggested might be taken from it. I think that, with the section as we have amended it, it is clear that if any shares are held by an agricultural association, or a municipal body or a school board, every member may vote by proxy.
I do not understand it in that way. I understand that proxies can only be exercised in favour of those bodies when they hold shares.
If that is the meaning it does not express it. If the section could be allowed to stand with the others I think an amendment might accomplish what my hon. friend desires it to accomplish.
I have no objection.

I move that the section be amended striking out the words in the second line ' when shares are ' and inserting in lieu thereof the words ' on shares ' so that it will read ' voting by proxy shall be allowed only on shares held by an agricultural association,' &c.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 29, district may be limited.

I think it would have been better to have put in the word ' shall ' instead of ' may ' in the second line. I therefore move that the word ' may ' in the second line be struck out and that the word ' shall ' be inserted in lieu thereof.
- Amendment agreed to.
I also move that in the last line the words ' canvassers or otherwise ' be struck out.
Amendment agreed to.

This is one of the crucial clauses of the Bill. Originally, this clause was limited distinctly to one electoral district. It is left now to the discretion of the Minister. By changing the word ' may ' to ' shall ' it would be so clear that any Minister of Finance would understand that he was expected to limit the distrifct within which any particular association can act. But it would still be within his power to give a license to one of these associations to cover a whole province. That ought not to be. . I sympathize very much with some of the things which have been said by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), in that particular. The York Loan Company has been instanced. In considering this Bill, one of the main things I would have in view would be to prevent anything like the York Loan happening, and if this Bill was properly drafted, the great losses which occurred on account of the York Loan, could not occur through an association incorporated under this Act. I still do not like that clause exactly as it reads. I think, if possible, there ought to be some way of so wording it, that the minister could not give a license to an association to act throughout a province. I think my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier is quite satisfied with that view of the case, but there is difficulty on account of the wording of it. Personally, I would prefer to see that clause further limited than it is at present.

There is no difficulty about the point raised by my hon. friend. The problem we had to cope with was how to limit it. It is very easy to say, for instance, that a society of this kind shall limit its operations to a parish or to a

counity, but it was pointed out that there are poor people in cities too, workingmen who might like to organize themselves into a co-operative loan and beneficial society, and it would be difficult to limit such a society by an electoral district, so we thought it best to allow the minister himself to fix the limit. For instance, in a city like Montreal or Toronto, the minister would say: Your operations are limited to the cities of Montreal or Toronto. It would be difficult to set down as a limit in the statute, the electoral district, but if it has to be limited, I have no objection if my hon. friend can suggest something.

There we come exactly to the danger I have been insisting on. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), has stated that I have been raising simply a shadow of a danger, that the operations of this Bill are going to be confined and are confined to small areas and districts. He now objects to the limitation because, forsooth, this must be made applicable to larger cities like Montreal and Toronto. If the Minister is. applied to for a license, under this Act for the organization of a company in Toronto or Montreal, or Winnipeg, or any large city, it would be almost impossible foT him to refuse a capitalization of two or three or five hundred thousand dollars. Here is an Act of which people are invited to make use. There are a lot of people in Toronto and Montreal who might apply under this Act to incorporate a company on the only scale that would be of any use in that district, and that at once gives the opportunity of perpetrating these frauds that I fear would take place.
There is no proxy in voting, each shareholder has the one vote.

For a small concern, that is quite right, but for a laTge concern, that gives the very power they want, they can control it, having seven votes, no matter how many others have. That is absolutely a danger in a large concern.
It has never been found to produce that effect anywhere in the world.
It would be found to produce it here very quickly, there is no doubt about that.

There is no objection to any clause limiting it in any way if any one will suggest the clause.	.
_ Mr. KING. In connection with the loans in cities, I think it desirable to make an observation that comes to my mind in connection with the remark of the hon. member for London (Mr. Beattie). He said that in all large cities there were any number of loan societies from which a man could obtain a loan. That is perfectly true, Mr. MONK.
if he has security to give, but what about the man whom this Bill is intended to make provision for, who had no other security to offer than his personal character, or the vouching of some personal friend, it will be seen that this suggestion does not apply. For instance, at the beginning of a building season a man engaged in a building trade may want to get a kit of tools. He may have no money to get the tools with, but he is known to the other members of the society; he goes to them and asks an advance without security, promising to pay back the money at the end of the year, or, perhaps, at the end of the building season. They know him, they have their money in the society and they say: We know you; we will advance this money to you. Then, at the end of the season, he pays back the loan he has had, with interest; but in the meantime he has been able to get his kit of tools and go on with his work. What man thus situated could get that loan from a loan society in a large city? That is -why it is important that this Act should apply to cities as well as to the country. For my part, I think_ it will be taken advantage of in the cities even more than in the country.

One of the great reasons advanced in support of this Bill was that this was to be applicable to country districts where members of the society would know each other, would have confidence in each other and would take each other's word. I have had some experience in city life and know something of mechanics. Mechanics are changing about constantly, and there could be no such combination among mechanics in cities. No good mechanic wants to borrow money to buy tools. The condition to be found in country districts where the members know one another's characters are not at all applicable to city life, to the great body of workmen.

My hon. friend certainly does not know anything about it, because there is nothing truer than what the minister has stated. It is in cities where cooperation exists that it does the chief good, and when I heard the member for London (Mr. Beattie) saying a moment _ ago that there -were plenty of loan companies in Ontario which could fulfil this mission it seemed to me that my hon. friend from London did not know very much about it, because down in Montreal, or in any other city, a workman who wants to purchase a set of tools, or to finish his house, or to buy a little lumber to commence the erection of a house, does jiot get that money from a loan company; the loan company would not give it to him; every one knows that. He will get it in these credit societies, where he is known, and the loan is made, not upon any security, because he has none to offer,

but on the guarantee of his moral character. So there is great need, indeed, of societies of this kind among the workingmen, or else why should they have asked yearly for the last ten years for the enactment of this legislation? Is it because they have loan companies in abundance prepared to furnish them with accommodation at a low rate? Evidently not. It is useful in the country parts and in the cities for the reason indicated by the minister, but I say again there is no objection to the Minister of Finance limiting the scope of each society. I think we ought to have some confidence in the party who is charged with the administration of the law. He can perform no end of fraud, but we have confidence in him; we manifest that confidence in statutes which we pass every day. Why should we not leave to the Secretary of State, who has charge of the administration of this law, the defining of the limits? Is he also dishonest? Is he necessarily going to perpetrate or lend himself to a fraud? It seems to me we may leave it to him, but if any one can suggest a way by which the scope of the society can be restricted there is no objection at all to such a restriction.

We have one of these societies in Montreal, and I know that it is doing a great deal of good, especially among the working people. Before it was established, any man who wanted to borrow a little money hatd to go to a money shark, and in order to get it he would sign almost anything. It was to prevent abuses of that kind that these societies were authorized under the provincial Act. The society lends money to poor men to buy homes or to furnish their houses, and the only guarantee it asks is the good-will of the borrower. This has worked so satisfactorily among the working people of Montreal that we have not found a single dishonest man borrowing money from the institution. This is due to the caution exercised by the committee or the board. This thing is demanded, not only by the working classes, but by the farmers. A number of men in Montreal have homes of their own which they would not have had but for this society. It has a charter under the provincial Act, but that is liable to be withdrawn at any moment, and we believe it would be more safe guarded under a federal Act. I know that all the hon. members of this House want to protect the workingmen, but some of them only look at one side of this measure, ignoring the good side of it. I do not think you will find, in Montreal or anywhere else in Canada, any workingmen who will be likely to act dishonestly in connection with one of these societies formed under this Act.
I propose that the following be added at the end of this section: ' But no society shall be allowed to do business over a greater area than that comprised in one electoral district.'

We had that proposition in the committee, and we could not agree to it there, because the head office of a company might be on the border of an electoral district, and there is no reason why its area of business should not extend across the border.

The argument of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier that we can surely trust the Secretary of State to carry out the Act, does not appeal to me with great force. It seems to me there ought to be something in the Act itself which would indicate the principle on which the rule should be applied. While the present Secretary of State may be quite familiar with what is intended by this law, after hearing the arguments here, there might be another Secretary of State at some future time who had not heard these arguments would be guided solely by what he found in the Act.

As pointed out by the hon. member^ for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt! there might be a group of men living side by side, divided only by a line defining an electoral district. In these cases some officers of the department would examine the application and report upon it to the minister. The minister is not likely to give his sanction without a careful examination of the situation, and it seems to me it would be safe enough to leave that measure of discretion with him.

There is nothing in the Bill to show that it was the intention of parliament that an association should be limited in its operations to a small section of the country, instead of being allowed to do business say over the whole province of Ontario.
Suppose the area were limited to a radius of ten miles from the office.
The words of the section indicate that it is the intention of parliament that the area should be restricted.
Suppose the Secretary of State decided to limit the area to the province of British Columbia. That would not be the intention of the Act.
I think the sense of responsibility of the minister would be sufficient to cause him to use great caution.

It seems to me that there is nothing in the wording of the section

to prevent a society, within the limits of the territory fixed by the minister, by means of circulars or newspaper advertis-ments, gathering in business from the ends of the earth, so that the Sheldon business might be repeated over and over again.

The sending out of circulars would not have any effect on the business
of the society, unless it brought about by an addition to the membership of the society, and the addition to the membership is circumscribed by the limitation which the minister puts on the business. If the minister decides that a society shall do business only in the city of Toronto, the sending of circulars all over Ontario would not have any effect, because only persons resident in Toronto could become members of the society. The fact is to be kept constantly in mind that operations are limited to persons resident in the district and who put their money into the society.

I do not think that in the Act it is provided that no one can be a member unless he resides within the limited area fixed under section 29. I do not believe there is any one in this House opposed to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier carrying out the object he seeks to accomplish, but I fear that he does not see the danger that may be contained in this measure. I think it would foe wise to refer this whole Bill back to the committee or at any rate such sections as are held over, and that the hon. memoer for Toronto (Mr. Osier) the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) and the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. King) should be members of that committee.

I cannot accept that proposition at all. A Co-operation Bill has been before parliament for nearly eight years and passed these stages on two or three occasions. Last year it was put through a very serious examination in the Committee on Banking and Commerce. This year it was agreed that we should take it up in Committee of the Whole and my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) even suggested that we should go on with the Bill reserving certain clauses for further consideration. To that I have no objection, but to ask that we should begin all that labour again is not fair to those who are promoting the Bill and is particularly unfair to the working classes who have asked for this legislation.
Where does the Minister of Labour get his authority for saying that membership must be restricted to a particular area defined by the minister?
The clause might restrict its business to a certain area.
But not its membership. The membership may foe gathered from all parts of the country.
That may be limited in the rules but is not in the Bill.

The Bill does not provide that the society cannot take any business or membership outside of that. Again there is a motion to strike out the words ' by means of agents, canvassers or otherwise.' That requires some thought. It seems to me that membership can be taken outside the district and if every member has a right to deposit, there are no restrictions as to where they shall get their deposits from or to whom they shall make loans.
I had in my mind that the words ' by means of agents, canvassers or otherwise ' would remain in the section.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On the amendment of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier these words were struck out.

There seemed to be so much difference about these co-operative societies that I thought it would foe well to get rid of the idea of canvassing. In Europe there is no provision limiting the operation of these societies to a particular locality. That would be considered absurd. I am not familiar with the English law but on the continent that idea never entered the minds of any one. The idea of limiting the operations of these societies has only originated in this country and this legislation is entirely new and strictly Canadian.
I would suggest that we should allow the section to stand as it is with these words in.
Add to that the suggestion of the hon. member tor Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) to which the hon. member for Jacques Cartier agreed and say that no man shall be a member unless he resides in the district.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendment in my hands is that the words ' no society shall be allowed to do business over a greater area than that comprised in one electoral district ' be added to the end of the section.

This is most objectionable. If these societies are beneficial they should not be limited to one electoral district. Take a small city with two representatives such as Hamilton, why arbitrarily limit the society to an electoral district. As the hon. member for North Oxford pointed out the head office of the company might be situated alongside another electoral district. Why, therefore,

limit it to the one? I should leave that to the discretion of the minister.

I would suggest that the clause toe reinstated in its original form and passed. We had all these arguments for hours before the committee and I remember distinctly that the word ' may ' was put in in place of ' shall ' because at times it would not be necessary for the minister to restrict, and we added purposely ' canvassers or otherwise ' so that they could not canvas by circulars. I would suggest that we leave the clause as it originally stood.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is moved that the clause read as follows:
The minister, by the certificate of incorporation and notice thereof in 'The Canada Gazette,' shall limit the district within which a society may carry on its business by means of offices or other places for carrying it on, or by means of agents, canvassers or otherwise.

Motion agreed to.
On section 31,
Every society shall lay aside at least ten per cent of its yearly net profits in order to establish a guarantee fund to meet losses, and until the said guarantee fund is equai to the maximum amount at any time of the paid-up share capital and deposits; and if the said maximum amount of paid-up capital and deposits is reduced by withdrawals the said fund shall be maintained at the said maximum amount notwithstanding such subsequent reduction, and the said yearly addition to net profits shall continue to be laid aside until the said guarantee fund has reached the aforesaid maximum amount of paid-up share capital and deposits, or in case the said fund is impaired by losses, after it has reached the said maximum, the said yearly addition shall be again laid aside until the said fund is completed.

I desire to state the circumstances under which this was added. I now remember that it was pointed out that in England, in a co-operative society that does any banking business, withdrawals are not allowed. There is a clause to that effect which the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) quoted a few moments ago. On the continent, it is the uniform rule to allow withdrawals without restriction in these credit and loan societies. There is also the fact that credit and loan societies have not been very successful in England, at any rate not as successful as on the continent. Co-operative trading societies in England have had an immense success, but the credit and loan feature has not been as successful as on the continent-I mean people have not gone into them in England as much as on the continent. We thought that this clause would be a fair compromise-to set aside ten per cent of the net
profits as a guarantee fund, that fund to be added to until it equals the total amount of paid-up capital. The shareholder is obliged to contribute to the guarantee fund, and, that done, withdrawals are allowed. I think that is a very fair compromise. The section was examined with great care last year.
I would suggest that, as we have held section 24 and as this section, number 31, relates to it in a way, we might let the section stand also to be considered when section 24 is taken up.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the consideration of section 31 be postponed? Carried.
On section 32,
A society shall invest its guarantee fund in public security of the government of Canada, or of a province thereof, or of a municipal corporation, school board or fabrique d'eglise, or may loan from such fund to such municipal or incorporated bodies upon the security of their general credit-

Suppose this society loans from its guarantee fund to a municipal body upon the security of its general credit, would that be regarded as reducing the guarantee fund below what is provided for in the previous section? Suppose the society had a guarantee fund of $1,000, and loaned $500 to a municipal corporation on the security of its general credit, would they have to make that up to meet the conditions?
On section 36,

I cadi attention to the first line of subsection 3:	' The board
should from time to time examine and audit.' It seems to me those words mean nothing. I would suggest: 'The board shall from time to time, and at least once in every quarter.'
That is provided for further on in the Bill by the yearly audit.

Does the hon. member think that is carrying out the intended meaning of section 3?	' The board should
from time to time ' would be considered to mean more frequently than once a year.

I have no objection to accept the hon. gentleman's suggestion. That is generally determined by the laws of the society.
Progress reported.
What will be taken up to-morrow, provided government orders are reached?
To-morrow is not a government day.
But suppose government orders are reached to-morrow, what do the government propose to take up.

There is very little op-portimity of reaching them with all these public orders on the Paper. But the Prime Minister left word that if government orders are reached, we will go on with civil government estimates.
